title: Words That Are Designed to Silence
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece addresses the tactic of using derogatory identity labels -- bigot, racist, sexist, and similar terms -- to shut down debate rather than engage with the substance of an argument. The author distinguishes between fairly calling out biased behavior, which is legitimate, and labeling a person's identity to stigmatize and silence them, which is not. Strong leaders, the piece argues, both refuse to wear such labels themselves and actively confront colleagues who deploy them against others. The goal is to keep disagreement focused on behaviors and facts rather than sweeping characterizations that chill honest speech. The piece frames eliminating identity labels as a prerequisite for genuinely open workplace dialogue.
points: Derogatory identity labels are sometimes used to silence opponents rather than win an argument on merit.
There's a real distinction between calling out biased behavior and labeling someone's identity to stigmatize them.
Strong leaders refuse to wear such labels and confront colleagues who use them on others.
Eliminating identity labels is treated as a precondition for genuinely open, candid debate.
quotes: When someone wants to chill your speech and place you in the jail cell of stereotypes, all they have to do is label you with a derogatory identity.
This has the intended effect of chilling their speech, at least temporarily, and diminishing their credibility.
Strong leaders reject labels and refuse to wear them. And they ask others to reject them, as well.
Strong leaders make unpopular decisions, give tough feedback, and engage in highly direct speech when necessary.
They don’t duck what they believe is the best course of action because others may not like them or disagree with their actions.
At the same time, they encourage others to push back respectfully.

They value the ability for everyone to debate and disagree with a leader’s actions and choices, knowing it is paramount for creating an open and inclusive workplace where all performance can be discussed objectively and candidly.

Occasionally, a team member who can’t or prefers not to win the argument or exert influence based on logic, evidence, or persuasive appeal will resort to labeling a leader or colleague as a means to denigrate their credibility and to curtail their speech.
